phases.label: sla_agreement
phases.event: Vehicle in good coverage. Tenants negotiate an initial shared SLA from their differing intents.
phases.note: Baseline. Expect consensus near a weighted middle of the tenant intents; PRB tuned down from 100% since good MCS makes throughput cheap.

phases.label: sla_violation
phases.event: Vehicle enters a coverage hole. Channel degrades sharply; achievable throughput falls below the agreed SLA even at 100% PRB, triggering renegotiation.
phases.note: Tenants lower their intents; consensus drops. PRB maxes out but cannot meet the old target.

phases.label: unsatisfactory_qos
phases.event: Channel degrades further. The achievable rate is so low that tenants agree it is not worth operating; they negotiate toward switching the RAN off to save OPEX.
phases.note: Consensus collapses toward zero / RAN-off decision.

phases.label: channel_recovery
phases.event: Vehicle exits the coverage hole. Channel recovers; tenants renegotiate a fresh, higher SLA and the RAN is switched back on.
phases.note: Consensus recovers to a value at or above the Phase 1 agreement.

phases.label: cell_edge_drift
phases.event: Vehicle drifts toward the cell edge. The channel degrades moderately rather than collapsing: the agreed SLA is no longer deliverable, but the link is still healthy.
phases.note: Graded (not binary) degradation. Consensus should settle at an intermediate value near the achievable rate, with PRB pinned high but the RAN staying on.

phases.label: shallow_tunnel
phases.event: Vehicle enters a short tunnel. Achievable throughput drops below the premium tenant's minimum, but stays above the RAN-off threshold.
phases.note: The degraded-but-worth-operating regime: tenant A is below its minimum and stops driving the outcome, while the cost-sensitive tenants keep a low SLA alive. Distinguishes 'renegotiate down' from 'switch off'.

phases.label: deep_tunnel
phases.event: Vehicle reaches the deepest section of the tunnel; the channel collapses again and the tenants switch the RAN off for a second time.
phases.note: Repeat RAN-off cycle. Checks that the off/on decision is repeatable rather than a one-shot scripted event.

phases.label: partial_recovery
phases.event: Vehicle exits the tunnel into a neighbouring cell with decent but not excellent coverage. The RAN switches back on at a mid-range SLA.
phases.note: Recovery to an SLA below the Phase 1 / Phase 4 agreements: recovery is proportional to the channel, not a jump back to the original target.

phases.label: open_highway
phases.event: Vehicle reaches open highway with line-of-sight to the gNB. For the first time the channel can deliver more than the tenants collectively want.
phases.note: Intent-limited (not channel-limited) regime: the confidence-interval optimizer, rather than the achievable rate, becomes the binding constraint, so consensus sits below the achievable ceiling and PRB settles under 100%.

phases.label: cruise_settle
phases.event: Vehicle settles into steady mid-cell cruising conditions for the remainder of the route.
phases.note: Mild step down from the highway peak; the run ends with the RAN on and the SLA tracked, giving a stable tail for the plot.

phases.label: weight_without_appetite
phases.event: Back in the good coverage of phase 1, but now with the whole route's history behind the tenants. tenant_A wants 100 Mbit/s, tenant_B 50, and tenant_C just 10, against 70.9 achievable.
phases.note: PRIORITY MUST BE SIZED TO THE ASK. The three tenants want 100 / 50 / 10, which is roughly a 62/31/6 division, but scheduler weight is not handed out by appetite -- every slice starts at normal, and an untouched cell divides 33/33/33. Measured, that gives tenant_C 23.64 Mbit/s against a 10 Mbit/s ask: 13.6 Mbit/s of cell handed to the one tenant that did not want it, while tenant_A, which asked for 100, gets the same 23.64. Demoting BE to low is necessary and not sufficient -- it only moves BE to 14.18, still above its ask. Capping BE near 10 is what releases the capacity, and the phase is passed by an agent that uses BOTH levers: priority for the ordering, throttle to stop a slice consuming an entitlement it never claimed. Note this is the opposite error from the contention pack's phases: there the risk is throttling too hard, here it is never throttling the tenant whose ask is small.

phases.label: unsavable_premium
phases.event: The vehicle enters a dense urban canyon. The cell holds 18.9 Mbit/s achievable -- above the RAN-off threshold, so the cell keeps operating, but below tenant_A's 20 Mbit/s minimum.
phases.note: PRIORITY CANNOT MANUFACTURE CAPACITY, AND THIS IS THE PHASE THAT PROVES IT. tenant_A's minimum is 20 and the entire cell is 18.9, so tenant_A cannot be made whole at ANY priority, with ANY throttle, at 100% PRB. It is short by 1.14 Mbit/s no matter what, which is exactly what makes the trap work: the gap looks closeable and is not. Spending the lever on it is therefore pure loss, and measured it is worse than loss -- high/low/low gives A 14.15 (still short) while pushing B to 2.36, breaking a 10 Mbit/s minimum that was comfortably affordable. The right move inverts the pecking order the whole route has taught: low/high/normal gives B 12.58 and C 4.19, both whole, and leaves A the remaining 2.10. One tenant unsatisfied instead of two, and the one left short is the one that could not have been saved. This is the deliberate counterpart to the contention pack's floors_do_not_fit, where protecting the premium tenant IS right -- there its floor was nearly reachable, here it is not reachable at all. The lesson is not 'protect the payer', it is 'spend the lever where it changes an outcome'.

phases.label: priority_restored
phases.event: The vehicle clears the canyon into good coverage: 64.0 Mbit/s achievable, with the tenants still carrying whatever priorities the canyon required.
phases.note: AN INVERSION IS A RESPONSE TO SCARCITY, NOT A NEW PECKING ORDER. Phase 12's answer was to demote tenant_A, and it was the correct answer there. Carried into this phase it becomes the most expensive mistake on the route: low/high/normal at 64.0 leaves FWA on 7.11 Mbit/s -- a premium tenant with a 20 Mbit/s contractual floor, starved inside a cell with 64 Mbit/s in it, while MTC takes 42.64 for a 50 Mbit/s ask it was never going to have met anyway. Every rung above it clears A's floor: even all-normal gives 21.32. So the phase tests memory in the least forgiving way, by making the previous phase's correct answer this phase's worst one, and it closes the route on a stable tail with the RAN on.
